title: Report on Studying Abroad at Duke University
paragraphs: For three months, from the end of May to early August 2013, I did clinical clerkships at Duke University in the United States. My clerkship departments were gastroenterology, bariatric medicine and nephrology. They were three months with far more failures than successes, but I learned a lot, and they also became the opportunity for me to greatly change the plans for my future that I had been picturing. I am very grateful to Nagoya University for giving me such a wonderful opportunity.

Now, on the first day of the clerkship, things did not go as I expected right from the start. I had been given the following instructions beforehand by email from the person in charge of the clerkship, so I tried to act accordingly.
Since both Jill and I will be away on Monday, please page Dr. *****at 9:30 AM on Monday and he will arrange to meet you and get you started in Hepatology. His pager is 919.***.****.

At 9:30 I called that number on the mobile phone I had bought just a few days earlier, but it did not connect. The phone's signal seemed to be terrible. And to begin with, I did not really understand what paging was. After flailing around for about ten minutes, I asked a passerby for help. It was Ann, a Nurse Practitioner. When I explained the situation, she helped me even though she was busy with her own work. She first tried to page from my phone, but it was in vain, so next we contacted Dr. ***** from her office. From Ann's computer she left a message on Dr. *****'s pager, and then Dr. ***** called Ann back. However, he told Ann that he was busy with a liver biopsy and that I should contact him directly, and hung up. I thought, "You could have used that call that was connected right now to talk to me," but I forcibly convinced myself, "Come to think of it, this is America, not Japan."

After that, Ann taught me how to contact Dr. ***** using the iPad I had and my mobile phone, whose functioning was doubtful, and I moved to the cafeteria, where the signal seemed to be good. By this time more than an hour had passed since I met Ann, and I could not bear to trouble her any more, so I told her of my gratitude and that I would manage the rest by myself. Then she said, "My son has also been to Japan, and I am sure he must have been looked after by Japanese people at that time." At that moment I strongly resolved that if I ever see a foreigner at a loss in Japan, I will help them thoroughly.

After saying goodbye to Ann, I immediately sent a message to Dr. *****'s pager from the iPad, but no call came back at all. There was nothing else to do, so I left the cafeteria thinking of going to the place where he was doing the liver biopsy. Before asking anyone, I tried to look for it myself using the signs, and after wandering around the hospital for about three minutes, I very luckily found what seemed to be the gastroenterology department office.

There again I explained my situation to the administrative staff and asked for help. The people who dealt with me were very kind, but it seems that not one person there knew that an exchange student from Japan was coming to gastroenterology. After many twists and turns, I was finally able to speak with Dr. ***** on the phone. Because it was my first day of the clerkship and I had not yet done the setup to view the electronic medical records, Dr. ***** told me, "If you can't access the electronic records, there's nothing for you to do, so why don't you do that setup today?" and the conversation ended. Of course I had no idea how to do that setup, but after more twists and turns I ended up being assigned to another doctor.

I think it was around 1 p.m. when I was able to reach that doctor. I had lunch, chatted with several doctors, and when it was about 2 p.m., I was told, "There's nothing in particular to see today, so you can go home," and I headed home. In this way I got through the first day safely, and from the next day the proper clerkship began.

I experienced many things in the three months of study abroad, but what remains in my memory is not so much medicine itself as experiences like the one above, being overcharged by a taxi driver, and a kind person who, perhaps pitying me for having been overcharged by a taxi driver, drove me for free a distance of 30 minutes each way, and so on. Come to think of it, it is obvious that if one were to learn only medicine, it would be overwhelmingly more efficient to study at Nagoya University in my native Japanese. Moreover, the medicine that a sixth-year medical student should learn is basic, and it should not be something that can only be done abroad. Nevertheless, the significance of deliberately studying abroad is, after all, things such as "seeing the wide world," "gaining international experience," "experiencing human kindness in a foreign land," and "continuing to act without getting discouraged even when you can't reach the doctor." I feel that through these experiences I was able to grow a little.
